title: Mā nas toke: spare our children, our life, our cattle and our men
theme: Rudra is asked not to harm the speakers in their children and descendants, their life, their cattle and horses, and not to strike their men in anger; they worship him with oblations and homage.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «तनयं तरुणं पुत्रम्» — the grown son

words.gram: verb, reduplicated aorist injunctive 2nd sg. active
past pass. part. m. nom. sg.
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «भामितोऽस्मदपराधैः कारितक्रोधः» — made angry by our offences
The anonymous commentator: «नमसा प्रणामेन» — with a bow

words.role: main verb of the last clause

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: naḥ before ā drops its visarga and stands in hiatus: na āyuṣi.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a; the a kept
sandhi.rule: naḥ before a becomes no, and the initial a of aśveṣu is kept, not elided: see sandhi exceptions.
vīrān keeps its n before m and is written joined.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant; after ī before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: bhāmitaḥ before v becomes bhāmito; vadhīḥ before h becomes vadhīr; haviṣmantaḥ before n becomes haviṣmanto.

sandhi_exceptions.note: naḥ aśveṣu is written no aśveṣu: the visarga becomes o, but the initial a is kept, as in the Ṛgveda’s text of this verse, where classical sandhi would elide it.

morphology.note: The locatives toke, tanaye, āyuṣi, goṣu, aśveṣu say in what respect the speakers are not to be harmed: ‘do not harm us in our children …’, a common Vedic construction with √riṣ.

Possessive adjective in -mat from haviṣ, ‘oblation’: ‘having oblations’, i.e. bringing them. The commentator: «यथाविधिनिष्पादितहविर्युक्तजुहूहस्ता वयं» — we, with ladles in hand holding the oblation prepared as prescribed.

translation.literal: Do not harm us in [our] offspring and descendant, us in [our] life, us in [our] cattle, us in [our] horses. Do not, O Rudra, angered, strike our men. Bearing oblations, we would worship you with homage.
translation.readable: Rudra, do not harm us in our children and grandchildren, in our lives, our cattle or our horses; even if we have angered you, do not strike our men. We come with offerings and bow to you.

anvaya: हे रुद्र नः तोके तनये मा रीरिषः नः आयुषि मा [रीरिषः] नः गोषु मा [रीरिषः] नः अश्वेषु मा रीरिषः । भामितः नः वीरान् मा वधीः । हविष्मन्तः [वयम्] नमसा ते विधेम ।
syntax: Four prohibitions in the first line, each mā naḥ with a locative of respect, the verb rīriṣaḥ coming once at the end. The second line has a further prohibition with its own verb (vadhīḥ) and object (vīrān), the vocative rudra and the participle bhāmitaḥ qualifying the god, then a closing optative (vidhema) with haviṣmantaḥ qualifying the speakers.

ambiguities.note: ‘Angered’ may describe Rudra as already angry or as one who might be angered; the commentator reads it as anger caused by our offences, «भामितोऽस्मदपराधैः कारितक्रोधः».

metre.name: jagatī
metre.note: As printed the first line has 24 syllables (12 + 12) and the second 22 (11 + 11): the last pāda, haviṣmanto namasā vidhema te, has eleven syllables where the jagatī norm is twelve. The Ṛgveda’s version of this pāda is different (see commentary).

beginner: This is the companion of the previous prayer and, like it, is addressed to Rudra. It asks him not to harm the speakers in the things on which a household depends: children and grandchildren, life itself, cattle and horses. It adds: even if you are angry, do not strike our men. It closes with the worshippers coming with offerings and bowing. The old commentator explains that the anger meant is anger caused by our own faults, and that the worshippers hold the ladles with the offering ready. The verse is also in the Ṛgveda and in the Śrī Rudram, where its last words differ. In this Upaniṣad it stands among the short prayers for protection before the offering formulas. The edition reports this and makes no claim about what reciting it achieves.
analogy: Like a farmer’s prayer before the season: name the children, the life of the house, the herds, and ask that none be lost.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Rudra not to harm the speakers in their offspring, their life, their cattle and their horses, and, though angered, not to strike their men; it ends with the speakers worshipping him with oblations and homage.

commentary.q: How does the commentator explain it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator takes the list as everything the speakers have: «एतदुपलक्षितमस्मदीयं सर्वस्व मा रीरिषः» — do not harm all that is ours, of which these are examples. The anger is anger caused by our own offences: «भामितोऽस्मदपराधैः कारितक्रोधः». The homage is a bow, «नमसा प्रणामेन», and the worship a sacrifice: «ते तवेज्यां विधेम कुर्याम».

commentary.q: How does it differ from the Ṛgveda?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Ṛgveda has the verse at 1.114.8. There the second word of life is āyau, «मा न आयौ», where the Mahānārāyaṇa has āyuṣi, both locatives of ‘life’; and the last pāda reads «हविष्मन्तःसदमित् त्वा हवामहे», ‘bearing oblations, we call on you always’, where this text has «हविष्मन्तो नमसा विधेम ते», ‘we would worship you with homage’.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among them). The anonymous bhāṣya explains the words and the rite; it does not argue an Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita position here, so the edition gives none.

parallels.note: The same verse in the Ṛgveda, in a hymn to Rudra; it reads āyau for āyuṣi and has a different last pāda (see commentary).

contemporary.text: The prayer admits that the god may be angry and that the speakers may be the cause, and asks that the consequences not fall on the household. Owning a fault while asking that others not suffer for it is a demanding stance. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Which of the things named here — children, life, livelihood — feels most fragile to you?
reflect.deeper: The commentator says the god’s anger is caused by our offences. How does that change the request ‘do not strike us’?
reflect.practice: When you are tempted to let someone else bear the cost of your mistake, name the mistake first.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 52–57 are missing from the digital text used here, and neither commentary file glosses these words; the edition’s concordance maps give no anuvāka of theirs for it. The anonymous bhāṣya is the only commentary quoted.
The verse is also in the tenth anuvāka of the Śrī Rudram (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.10), in this library’s Śrī Rudram edition.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text has रीरिषः (the last word of 10.52) at the start of this anuvāka: a boundary difference in that e-text, not a different reading. The Ānandāśrama text’s प्ना for मा is a misprint (corrections.json).
